records.p: A small, slender rat with a pointed muzzle, rounded ears and reddish-brown upper fur. The hind foot is pale except for a dark outer margin near the ankle, a useful distinguishing feature (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Pacific Rat is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Dinagat, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo, and Misamis Oriental. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Pacific Rat uses scrub, forest and cultivated land and can climb trees while foraging. Its diet includes seeds, fruit, other plant material and invertebrates, with mainly nocturnal activity (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Mus exulans (T. R. Peale, 1849). Its historical type locality is Tahiti Island (France), Society Islands (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 282.9 g for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Brown Rat has been documented on Leyte, including Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013). The Brown Rat commonly occupies settlements, cultivated land and other disturbed habitats. It eats both plant and animal material; forest appears among the working checklist’s broad categories without evidence that the species is a native forest specialist (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled traits describe ground foraging, nocturnal activity, and a varied diet of seeds, fruit, other plant material and invertebrates (Wilman et al., 2014). Comparative reproductive data report litters with multiple young (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Mus Norvegicus (J. Berkenhout, 1769). Its historical type locality is "Great Britain." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Asian House Rat has variable dark-brown to grey dorsal fur, and the tail is typically as long as or longer than the head and body. These external characters describe the regional field-guide concept but are insufficient alone to distinguish every similar Rattus species (Jumawan et al., 2024). The East Asian House Rat has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Misamis Oriental, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The East Asian House Rat uses farmland, other disturbed environments and some forest settings, as recorded in a small-mammal survey in Bukidnon (Rizalda & Buenavista, 2026). Compiled dietary traits include seeds, invertebrates, fruit, and other plant material, with ground foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Mus tanezumi (Temminck, 1844). Its historical type locality is "japonais est Ta-nezumi." Interpreted by J. K. Jones, Jr. and D. H. Johnson in 1965 as "Japan... vicinity of Nagasaki on the southern island of Kyushu." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: This stocky moss mouse has relatively long, somewhat harsh fur. The back is rich brownish chestnut, grading toward buffy-brown underparts, with dark brown feet and tail. In the 2024 comparison of Mindanao Tarsomys, its pelage is longer and less spiny than that of T. echinatus, and its skull is larger than that of T. orientalis (Rickart et al., 2024). The Dusky Moss Mouse has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Dusky Moss Mouse inhabits forest on Mindanao and forages on the ground. Mount Kitanglad stomach samples contained plant material and small amounts of arthropods; this differs from the invertebrate-only estimate in a compiled trait dataset (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Tarsomys apoensis (Mearns, 1905). Its historical type locality is Mount Apo, 2058 m, Mindanao Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A stocky moss mouse with short, distinctly spiny dorsal fur, brownish-grey upperparts and a much paler greyish-white underside. Some examined specimens show a white midventral patch. Compared with T. apoensis, it has a shorter, harsher coat and paler feet and ears; its tail scales are comparatively large (Rickart et al., 2024). The Spiny Moss Mouse has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Matutum (GBIF.org, 2026). The Spiny Moss Mouse is associated with forests. EltonTraits characterizes it as a terrestrial forager on invertebrates, with activity spanning several parts of the day; species-level regional observations are needed to test those compiled patterns locally (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, ground foraging and nocturnal, crepuscular and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Tarsomys echinatus (Musser & Heaney, 1992). Its historical type locality is Balisong, 823–1128 m, Tupi, Mount Matutum, South Cotabato Province, southern Mindanao Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The original description characterizes Tarsomys orientalis as a relatively small earthworm mouse with dense, soft, dark brown to blackish dorsal fur, contrasting with the coarse, spiny pelage of T. echinatus. Diagnosis also considers the short tail, narrow hind feet and cranial characters, rather than pelage color alone (Rickart et al., 2024). The Kampalili Moss Mouse is known from forest habitats on Mount Kampalili in eastern Mindanao, with records from the Davao Oriental and Davao de Oro sides of the mountain (Rickart et al., 2024). The Kampalili Moss Mouse has been recorded in lower montane and mossy forest on Mount Kampalili, sheltering among roots, moss, leaf litter and woody debris (Rickart et al., 2024). The species was originally described as Tarsomys orientalis (Rickart, Rowsey, Ibañez, Quidlat, Balete, & Heaney, 2024). Its historical type locality is "2 km S, 2 km W Kampalili peak, Maragusan Municipality, Compostela Valley Province [now Davao de Oro Province], Philippines, 1,900 m elevation, 7.2866°N, 126.2753°E" (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao rapid color guide lists head-and-body length of 77–102 mm, tail length 53–76 mm and hind-foot length 24–29 mm for this squirrel (Heaney et al., n.d.). The Philippine Pygmy Squirrel has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Basilan, and Leyte, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Capotoan on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Pygmy Squirrel is associated with upland habitats. Trait data describe arboreal, diurnal foraging, and stomach samples from Mount Kitanglad contained plant and arthropod remains (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). In 2 stomachs examined from Mt. Kitanglad, researchers recorded plant material in 100% and arthropod remains in 100% (Heaney et al., 2006, Table 5). EltonTraits estimates a diet of other plant material (80%), invertebrates (20%), with arboreal foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). PanTHERIA compiles litter size 1.9 for comparison (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Sciurus concinnus (O. Thomas, 1888). Its historical type locality is Isabela, Basilan Island, Zamboanga Province, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Field Museum Mindanao guide reports head-and-body lengths of 290–305 mm, tails of 280–295 mm and hind feet of 55–60 mm for this flying squirrel (Heaney et al., n.d.). The Basilan Flying Squirrel has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kalatungan Range, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Basilan Flying Squirrel uses lowland and montane forest, foraging at night in trees. Compiled traits describe a diet that includes fruit, seeds and other plant material (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sciuropterus crinitus (Hollister, 1911). Its historical type locality is "Basilan I, Philippines." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao Flying Squirrel is a comparatively large member of Petinomys, with grizzled chestnut-brown fur above and buff to buff-brown below. Institutional descriptions note small, rather bare ears with long tufts of hair. Historical comparative material distinguishes its larger skull and round, rather than strongly flattened, tail from P. crinitus. Identification should incorporate body measurements and verified geographic comparison, not coat colour alone (National Institute of Biological Resources, n.d.). The Mindanao Flying Squirrel has been documented on Mindanao, including Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Flying Squirrel inhabits forest, moves through the canopy at night, and feeds on fruit, seeds and other plant material (Monograph of the Family Sciuridae, n.d.; Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sciuropterus mindanensis (Rabor, 1939). Its historical type locality is "Badiangon, Gingoog, Oriental Misamis Province, northern coast of Mindanao, Philippines." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: A published species account in Wilson, Lacher and Mittermeier (2016) describes the Davao Squirrel as having buff-colored cheeks and a darkening stripe along the middle of the back from the nose to the tail base. Hairs in that dorsal stripe have dark bases and russet tips. The belly is apricot-buff, with a clear transition between the darker back, sides and paler underside. The central tail is described as russet, edged with black and then white, and the underside of the tail is less russet. The account reports male mean head-and-body length of 198 mm and mean tail length of 182 mm, without specifying the sample size in the accessible treatment. These are published external recognition characters, not a demonstrated unique diagnosis against other Philippine Sundasciurus. Sanborn (1952) named the taxon from Madaum in the Tagum area of Davao, and Wilson and Reeder (2005) noted possible conspecificity with S. mindanensis, S. philippinensis and S. samarensis. Until voucher-based comparative diagnosis and the species boundary are resolved, do not label an ordinary Mindanao squirrel as S. davensis solely from location, coloration or apparent size. The Davao Squirrel has been documented on Mindanao (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The Davao Squirrel is associated with forests. Trait data describe chiefly daytime activity, a substantial fruit component in the diet and foraging that includes the ground; these traits are compiled rather than measurements from a specific Davao study (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit, other plant material, and invertebrates, with ground foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Callosciurus davensis (Sanborn, 1952). Its historical type locality is "Madaum, 25 feet [8 m] altitude, Tagum Municipality, Davao Province, Mindanao Island, Philippines Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

In a historical review of Mindanao specimens treated as Sciurus cagsi, now included under Sundasciurus mindanensis, Meyer described a bushy tail mottled reddish brown, black and white above, brown beneath with a black stripe along each side, and white margins and tip. A reddish colour at the tail base was also emphasized. Meyer reported disagreement between Steere’s original description of S. mindanensis and the specimens he examined, especially in the colour of the feet and tail. These historical traits describe the material examined, not a validated identification key for every modern Mindanao squirrel (Meyer, 1896; American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The Mindanao Squirrel has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Squirrel is associated with forests and cultivated areas. EltonTraits describes mainly daytime foraging and a diet of fruit, other plant matter and some invertebrates; the compilation does not determine how frequently the species uses either habitat in Greater Mindanao (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit, other plant material, and invertebrates, with ground foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sciurus Mindanensis (Steere, 1890). Its historical type locality is Mindanao I (Philippines) (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao rapid color guide gives head-and-body length of 174–210 mm, tail length of 130–205 mm and hind-foot length of 37–52 mm. Identification among squirrels still requires plumage and other traits (Heaney et al., n.d.). A Hijo Forest species profile describes dark-brown dorsal pelage with paler hair tips and grayish to light-brown underparts, while warning that pelage color varies geographically (Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Tree Squirrel has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Malindang Range, Bega Watershed, and Sultan Kudarat. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Tree Squirrel is associated with montane habitats. Its compiled ecological traits describe diurnal foraging and a diet comprising fruit, other plant material and a smaller invertebrate component (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit, other plant material, and invertebrates, with ground foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sciurus Philippinensis (G. R. Waterhouse, 1839). Its historical type locality is "Mindanado (= Mindanao I)," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 225.0 g and head–body length 210.0 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Samar Squirrel has records from Samar and Leyte. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Samar Squirrel is associated with forests and agricultural areas. Trait data describe daytime activity and feeding on fruit, other plant material and some invertebrates, but provide no habitat-use comparison between Samar and Leyte (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit, other plant material, and invertebrates, with ground foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sciurus Samarensis (Steere, 1890). Its historical type locality is "Samar and Leyte," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao Treeshrew has a long tapering snout, large eyes, a slender squirrel-like body and an elongated, fully furred tail. It can be distinguished from rodents at close range by its narrow pointed face, although photographs of an isolated animal may not provide enough scale for unequivocal identification. The National Museum describes the species under Tupaia everetti and notes that the older name Urogale everetti was replaced following a molecular phylogenetic study (National Museum of the Philippines, 2022). The Mindanao Treeshrew has been documented on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo, Mount Lumot, Mount Toloma, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Heaney et al., 2006). The Mindanao Treeshrew uses secondary lowland forest on Dinagat, where a nest was documented in a cavity at the base of a dead pandan tree (Senarillos & Ibañez, 2023). In 8 stomachs examined from Mt. Kitanglad (reported as Urogale everetti), researchers recorded plant material in 12%, arthropod remains in 100%, and earthworm material in 50% (Heaney et al., 2006, Table 5). The species was originally described as Tupaia Everetti (O. Thomas, 1892). Its historical type locality is "Zamboanga, W. Mindanao, Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 uses the combination Tupaia everetti following a generic transfer from Urogale, a name commonly encountered in older Mindanao field guides and mammal surveys (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).
